name: Tulip Festival, Srinagar
image_query: Indira Gandhi Memorial Tulip Garden Srinagar
when: Late March to April, dates set each year by the Floriculture Department
summary: Each spring the Indira Gandhi Memorial Tulip Garden, about 30 ha at the foot of the Zabarwan range above Dal Lake, blooms with over a million tulips in dozens of varieties. The garden's annual Tulip Festival is Kashmir's biggest spring event and the start of the tourist season.
body: The garden was opened in 2007 on the slopes once known as Siraj Bagh, between the Zabarwan hills and Dal Lake, and is often described as the largest tulip garden in Asia. Terraced beds are planted in long colour bands with tulips, plus hyacinths, daffodils and ranunculus. The first bulbs came from the Netherlands, and the garden now holds around 70 tulip varieties.

The festival runs while the flowers last, usually three to four weeks from late March or early April, with cultural programmes, Kashmiri food stalls and handicraft displays organised by the tourism and floriculture departments. Bloom timing depends on the weather, and a warm spell can bring it forward by a week or more.

Expect large crowds, especially on weekends and holidays, when hundreds of thousands of visitors pass through in a season. Pair the visit with the nearby Mughal gardens of Chashme Shahi, Nishat and Shalimar, which are also at their spring best, and with almond blossom at Badamwari if you come in March.
tips: Go at opening time on a weekday; by late morning the paths are packed.
Check the official opening date each year before booking flights; bloom varies with the weather.
Combine with Chashme Shahi next door and Nishat Bagh in the same morning.

faqs.q: When is the Srinagar tulip festival in 2026?
faqs.a: The tulip garden usually opens in the last week of March or the first days of April, and the festival runs for three to four weeks while the flowers last. Exact dates are announced each year by the Floriculture Department. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is the entry fee for the tulip garden?
faqs.a: In recent seasons adults have paid about ₹75–100 and children less, with tickets at the gate or online. Fees can change each year. Carry ID and cash or UPI, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much time do I need at the tulip garden?
faqs.a: One and a half to two hours is enough to walk the terraces and take photographs. Add an hour for Chashme Shahi next door. Arrive at opening to avoid the midday crowds.

faqs.q: Is the tulip garden suitable for seniors and wheelchairs?
faqs.a: The garden is terraced with paths and some slopes and steps. Seniors can manage the lower terraces comfortably. Wheelchair access is partial; ask at the gate about accessible routes, and avoid peak hours.

name: Kheer Bhawani Mela, Tulmulla
summary: The annual mela at the Kheer Bhawani temple in Tulmulla, about 25 km north-east of Srinagar in Ganderbal district, is the most important gathering for Kashmiri Pandits. Pilgrims offer kheer, rice pudding, to the goddess Ragnya Devi at a sacred spring under old chinar trees.
body: The temple honours Kheer Bhawani, also called Ragnya Devi, the protective goddess of many Kashmiri Hindu families. Her shrine stands in the middle of a seven-sided spring at Tulmulla, surrounded by water channels and ancient chinars. Devotees believe the spring changes colour, and that darker shades foretell difficult times. The present temple was built by Maharaja Pratap Singh in the 1910s and later renovated by Maharaja Hari Singh.

On Jyeshtha Ashtami, the eighth day of the bright half of the lunar month of Jyeshtha, thousands of pilgrims gather to offer milk, kheer and flowers, sing bhajans and share meals. Many Kashmiri Pandits travel back to the valley for the day, and local Muslim neighbours traditionally help with flowers, milk and stalls.

Visitors are welcome to attend respectfully. Expect security arrangements, crowds and traffic on the Ganderbal road. The temple is also lovely on ordinary days, especially early in the morning, and can be combined with the drive to Sonamarg.
tips: Arrive early in the morning before the main crowds and heat.
Remove leather items and shoes where asked, and dress modestly.
Combine an ordinary-day visit with the drive to Sonamarg on the same road.

faqs.q: When is the Kheer Bhawani mela?
faqs.a: It falls on Jyeshtha Ashtami in the Hindu lunar calendar, usually in late May or June. The exact date changes each year. Check current status and any yatra arrangements announced by the administration before you travel.

faqs.q: How far is Kheer Bhawani from Srinagar?
faqs.a: The temple is at Tulmulla in Ganderbal district, about 25 km north-east of Srinagar, roughly 45 minutes to an hour by road. Shared vehicles run to Ganderbal; a private taxi is easiest on mela day.

faqs.q: Can non-Hindus visit Kheer Bhawani temple?
faqs.a: Visitors of all backgrounds can usually visit respectfully, outside restricted areas. Dress modestly, remove shoes, avoid leather in the inner area and follow priests' instructions. Photography rules vary; ask before taking pictures.

faqs.q: What is offered at Kheer Bhawani?
faqs.a: Devotees offer kheer, a rice and milk pudding, along with milk, sugar candy and flowers, poured into the sacred spring. Offerings are available at stalls near the temple. Please do not throw plastic or packaging into the spring.

name: Amarnath Yatra
when: July–August, in the month of Shravan, ending on Shravan Purnima (Raksha Bandhan)
summary: Each summer, pilgrims walk to the Amarnath cave at 3,888 m to see a natural ice lingam venerated as Shiva. The yatra starts from Chandanwari near Pahalgam on the 43 km southern route, or from Baltal near Sonamarg on the shorter 13 km northern route, and shapes travel across Kashmir in July and August.
body: The Amarnath cave lies in a high side valley about 141 km from Srinagar. Inside, water freezes into a stalagmite that devotees worship as a Shiva lingam. The yatra is organised by the Shri Amarnathji Shrine Board with the government, over a season of several weeks in the month of Shravan, traditionally ending on Shravan Purnima, the day of Raksha Bandhan.

The southern route from Pahalgam goes by road to Chandanwari, then on foot via Sheshnag and Panchtarni, about 43 km and three to five days return. The northern route from Baltal is about 13 km and can be done in one or two days. Ponies, palkis and helicopter services to Panchtarni operate under official rates.

Advance registration, a compulsory health certificate from an authorised doctor and RFID cards are required, and the trail climbs above 4,000 m at Mahagunas pass. Pilgrims should acclimatise, carry warm and waterproof clothing, and talk to their doctor before travelling. Non-pilgrims should expect convoys and restrictions on the Pahalgam and Sonamarg roads.
tips: Register early with the Shrine Board; slots for popular dates fill fast.
Get the compulsory health certificate from an authorised doctor before registering.
If you are not a pilgrim, avoid Pahalgam and Sonamarg roads on convoy mornings.

faqs.q: How do I register for the Amarnath Yatra?
faqs.a: Registration opens months before the yatra through the Shri Amarnathji Shrine Board's official channels and designated banks. You need a compulsory health certificate from an authorised doctor and photo ID, and you collect an RFID card before the yatra. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Which Amarnath route is easier, Pahalgam or Baltal?
faqs.a: Baltal is shorter, about 13 km one way, but steeper, and can be done in one or two days. The Pahalgam route via Chandanwari, Sheshnag and Panchtarni is about 43 km, longer but more gradual, and takes three to five days return.

faqs.q: What is the altitude of Amarnath cave?
faqs.a: The cave is at about 3,888 m, and the southern route crosses Mahagunas pass above 4,000 m. Altitude sickness is a real risk. Acclimatise, ascend slowly, drink water and talk to your doctor before the yatra, especially if you have heart or lung conditions.

faqs.q: Can tourists visit Pahalgam during the Amarnath Yatra?
faqs.a: Yes, but expect heavy security, traffic restrictions and limited access to Chandanwari and some areas. Hotels fill with pilgrims and prices rise. If you want a quiet Pahalgam stay, plan for May, June or September instead.
